item.title: Drake’s Dissing Somebody On “Ya Hit,” But Who?
item.dc:creator: Chuck Creekmur (@ChuckCreekmur)
item.description: Drake’s appearance on Future’s “Ya Hit” includes a jab at somebody, but who?
item.content:encoded:
Drake sounds ready to send somebody’s unfinished album straight to the clearance rack on “Ya Hit.”

The Toronto rapper appears on Future’s newly released single alongside Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy. The record arrived November 6, giving Hip-Hop a substantial reunion to discuss before anybody even starts examining the lyrics. 

Naturally, I have questions about the lyrics.

“Your album ain’t gettin’ no better,” Drake raps. The target is unidentified. So now we have a mystery.

Imagine spending months adjusting the drums, replacing features and debating cover art, only for somebody to suggest the problem is the album itself. That is remarkably impolite.

But who deserves that review? Not Kendrick.

There is no answer. We certainly can assume a few people, however I’ll refrain from naming names. A familiar grudge makes this too easy. Drake could be addressing somebody specific. He could also be delivering competitive rap talk with enough ambiguity to keep everybody guessing. Maybe it’s only a Sucker MC.

Personally, I find the setting almost as intriguing as the jab. Future has Drake and Travis on the same release, and the temptation is to treat that musical reunion as a complete explanation of their relationships. A song can tell us they worked together. This reunion is overshadowed by the mysteries.

That is especially worth remembering when listeners start assigning enemies to an unnamed target. A collaboration confirms a collaboration. The rest needs its own receipts.

Still, the album reference gives this particular line some bite. Drake is questioning somebody’s judgment about their own work, which feels more dismissive than a routine boast about being the best. My reading? He sounds less interested in a lengthy argument than in telling somebody to stop asking for another extension.

For now, AllHipHop fans have a new record and an unresolved question. Enjoy the reunion, examine the verse and keep the theories labeled.

item.title: Chris Brown Pushes Back As Atlanta Concert Chaos Fuels Usher Feud Rumors
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chris Brown responded after fans criticized his delayed Atlanta concert with Usher and speculated about tension between the singers.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Brown appeared to push back on online chatter after fans blasted the opening night of his five-show Atlanta run with Usher.

TMZ reported that Thursday’s show at Mercedes-Benz Stadium started around 10 P.M., roughly two and a half hours later than expected. Concertgoers also complained that the singers did not perform a song together and that large portions of the planned set were cut.

The reaction was immediate. Some fans demanded refunds, described the performance as rushed and said they would not buy another ticket for either artist. One attendee called the show “very underwhelming.”

The complaints went beyond the wait. People who paid for a co-headlining show expected Brown and Usher to share the stage. Without those moments, the shorter sets felt even more noticeable.

The missing duets quickly turned a production problem into a rumor about the two headliners. Fans speculated that tension backstage explained the late start and shortened show, but no confirmed evidence of a dispute has surfaced.

Brown posted a brief message to his Instagram Story as the talk spread: “Internet cap. don’t fall for it.” He did not identify a specific claim, leaving it unclear whether he meant the feud rumors, the concert complaints or both.

The rough first night arrived during what should have been a victory lap. Brown and Usher are the first artists to play five shows during one tour stop at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, passing the four-show mark Beyoncé set in 2025.

The Atlanta dates followed a strong commercial stretch. AllHipHop reported last week that Brown and Usher became the first co-headliners to top Billboard’s monthly touring chart after grossing $77.4 million in September.

The pair expanded the tour to 59 shows in August as demand climbed. They later canceled several October dates, with organizers citing the health and well-being of the performers and crew.

That history made Atlanta’s opening night stand out. The tour had already proven it could sell stadiums and deliver a long run. This time, fans left talking about what was missing, not the milestone.

Four Atlanta concerts remained on the schedule after Thursday’s opener, giving Brown and Usher another chance to deliver the joint moments fans expected. Neither singer had issued a detailed explanation for the delay or shortened set.

item.title: Tay-K’s Prison Album Raises Big Questions About Money & Monsters
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Tay-K’s forthcoming album invites a lot of drama ahead of its November streaming debut.
item.content:encoded:
Tay-K has announced a new jailhouse album.

The project was assembled through prison phone collaborations in Texas in a last ditch effort to reclaim control of his artistic expression.

The rapper’s #MonstersUnderMyBed is scheduled for release Nov. 13 following three years of development with producers John Cunningham and Warpstr. Its announcement accompanied the single “F**K U,” which explores his childhood and subsequent incarceration.

The recording process begs the question: How much control does an incarcerated artist have over music completed by collaborators outside prison?

Tory Lanez has a potential blueprint for Tay-K’s recording process through his Prison Tapes series, which launched in July 2024. Lanez said he and his engineer developed a way to record vocals over a jail telephone while preserving what he described as professional sound quality after repeated attempts. He transformed telephone recordings into commercially released songs.

Tay-K’s announcement describes sustained telephone collaboration but does not explain how vocals were captured or how the recordings were edited

Ultimately Tay-K hopes the project will “reclaim [his] right to artistic expression that was manipulated by the justice system.”

That statement places artistic agency at the center of the rollout. Establishing how that agency worked would require details about who selected takes, approved production changes and authorized the final versions. The announcement describes the collaboration without documenting those decisions.

The new single follows “PUNCH YOU DOWN,” “Everywhere I Go” and “Erupt.” Tay-K managed to produce “F**K U” with Cunningham and Warpstr.

His recent activity also includes an appearance on “SPOTLIGHT / INNER CHILD,” the closing track on Dominic Fike’s How to Quit Smoking. According to the supplied report, that contribution similarly addresses childhood experiences.

Tay-K received an 80-year sentence in April 2025 following his murder conviction in the death of Mark Anthony Saldivar.

A judge ordered that punishment to run concurrently with his earlier 55-year sentence.

item.title: Jeezy Says Hip-Hop Elders Failed Young Rappers Who Needed Help
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jeezy says Hip-Hop elders failed young rappers by missing their pain, leaving too few mentors as violence and trauma took hold.
item.content:encoded:
Jeezy believes his generation of Hip-Hop leaders failed young rappers by hearing the anger in their music without paying enough attention to the pain underneath it.

The Atlanta veteran delivered that blunt assessment during a new All The Smoke conversation with Matt Barnes and Stephen Jackson.

The discussion turned to drill music, violence and the lack of trusted adults available to artists coming up in neighborhoods where survival often comes before long-term planning.

“I think they don’t got no outlets,” Jeezy said. He argued that many young artists also lack the older voices who once pulled him aside and challenged his choices.

Jeezy pointed to T.I., who once made him decide whether he wanted a future in music or the streets.

He also remembered Jay-Z giving him a hard business lesson when he needed one. Those conversations did not solve every problem, but they showed him that somebody with experience was paying attention.

He said the music young rappers make reflects the places around them. In his view, the problem is not simply that artists are choosing the wrong message. It is that violence can make a person feel important when the rest of the world has made him feel invisible.

Money can be earned again, Jeezy warned, but a lost life or a prison sentence cannot be reversed. That is why he wants veterans to do more than criticize the sound or shake their heads at the consequences.

“When they was telling us they was hurt, we wasn’t paying attention. And now they’re acting out,” he said.

The position is consistent with a responsibility Jeezy claimed more than a decade ago.

In a 2015 AllHipHop interview, he said, “It’s on me to give the younger cats the game, because when you got in this game I told you how to trap or die.”

His own path now includes family, books and a Las Vegas residency with a live orchestra. Jeezy presented that growth as proof the story doesn’t have to end where it began. His larger point was that established artists cannot wait until a tragedy to offer the guidance they had the power to give earlier.

item.title: The Weeknd Ends “After Hours Til Dawn Tour” With $1.3 Billion Gross
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: The Weeknd finished After Hours Til Dawn with more than $1.3 billion in ticket sales after a four-year stadium tour.
item.content:encoded:
The Weeknd finished his “After Hours Til Dawn” tour with more than $1.3 billion in ticket sales, closing a four-year run that drew over 9 million fans across five continents, according to promoter Live Nation.

The tour concluded in Kuala Lumpur at TM Stadium Nasional, the company announced. Its final count covered 176 shows in 67 cities across 30 countries, beginning with the tour’s July 2022 launch.

The final figure extended a record The Weeknd had already claimed. AllHipHop reported that “After Hours Til Dawn” passed $1 billion in November 2025, when it became the highest-grossing tour by a male solo artist.

The $1.3 billion figure was the final reported gross for the completed run.

Variety reported that the promoter-confirmed total placed the tour third overall behind Taylor Swift’s “Eras Tour,” which topped $2 billion, and Coldplay’s “Music Of The Spheres” tour, which exceeded $1.5 billion.

Elton John’s farewell tour previously held the male solo record at $939 million.

The Weeknd’s 2026 dates alone brought in more than $500 million from over 3 million tickets.

July accounted for over $120 million and nearly 900,000 tickets, according to the promoter.

The last stretch took the production through Asia, a market Live Nation’s touring president Omar Al-joulani described as a major remaining step for the singer.

“The Weeknd has been a stadium act in Australia, South America, Mexico and all through Europe, so Asia was the final frontier,” Al-joulani told HITS Daily Double.

The Asian leg grew from 11 dates to 17 sold-out shows, including three in Bangkok and four in Hong Kong.

The Hong Kong stop also connected the tour to a new release. The Weeknd introduced “Hong Kong” during his opening Kai Tak Stadium show on October 24.

Released October 31 in East and Southeast Asia, the song used vocals from Faye Wong’s 1993 track “Monsoon.”

The stadium records stretched beyond Asia. His seven SoFi Stadium shows set male-artist records for performances and gross. Six Rogers Centre dates set a male solo record for a single tour. Seven U.K. shows in 2026 drew more than 450,000 fans.

Live Nation also reported $8.5 million raised through the XO Humanitarian Fund and Global Citizen across the run.

That included $3 million in 2026 for work through the World Food Programme and Global Citizen supporting hunger relief, education and women and girls.

item.title: Wyclef Jean Talks “The Greatest” Muhammad Ali & Why He And Ms. Lauryn Hill Are Superheroes
item.dc:creator: Quierra Luck
item.description: The Fugees co-founder checks in with Quierra Luck on writing the theme song for Prime Video's "The Greatest," the Quincy Jones rule he still follows and where he and Lauryn Hill stand now.
item.content:encoded:
Wyclef Jean has never played it safe. He draped a Haitian flag over his shoulder on the Grammys stage, ran for president of his home country and spent three decades blending genres the industry worked hard to keep apart. So when Prime Video needed a theme for its Muhammad Ali series, it makes sense the call went to the Fugees’ resident rebel.

“Gladiator,” which Jean co-wrote with series creator Ben Watkins and performs with Ghanaian-Jamaican singer Kofi Black, is the theme for “The Greatest,” the eight-episode limited series on Ali that premiered Nov. 4. Jean wasn’t chasing a soundtrack placement. He wanted a real theme, the kind Quincy Jones taught him to write, a record that sticks with you long after the credits roll.

For Jean, Ali isn’t just a subject. He’s a blueprint. The two first crossed paths in the ’90s, when the Fugees jumped on “Rumble in the Jungle,” and Jean says Ali’s willingness to take unpopular stands shaped everything from “If I Was President” to his own run for office in Haiti. In his eyes, Ali was a gladiator, someone who bled for his people in and out of the ring. Or as Jean puts it, “Death is scared of the gladiator.”

The timing matters, too. It’s been 30 years since the Fugees cooked up “The Score” in a basement in the hood and changed the sound of the decade. Jean is fresh off a London run celebrating the album, midway through his plan to drop seven albums this year and, he says, back on the same wavelength as Lauryn Hill.

AllHipHop caught up with Jean the day before “The Greatest” premiered to talk Ali, the Quincy Jones lesson behind “Gladiator,” the night he turned the Grammys into a moment of Haitian pride and why nobody gets to put him in a box.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

‘He’s a true gladiator’

AllHipHop: How did “Gladiator” come about?

Wyclef Jean: I have a heavy background in composing for film. I did the score for “Life” with Eddie Murphy and Martin Lawrence and wrote the theme for “Hotel Rwanda.” And my relationship with Muhammad Ali goes back to the Fugees doing “Rumble in the Jungle.” I don’t think I could have written “If I Was President,” or run for president of my country, if it wasn’t for Ali. So when I got the call, I felt like I had a cheat code.

AllHipHop: How do you capture someone as larger than life as Ali in one song?

Wyclef Jean: The word gladiator captures it. A gladiator sacrifices himself for the arena. There’s no greater sacrifice than saying, “I’ll take the fall for another human.” A gladiator is defiant. Death is scared of the gladiator. Ali could have been comfortable, and he decided, nah, I’ve got to fight for my people. Not just in words, but in action. He’s a true gladiator.

AllHipHop: You ran for president of Haiti. Did you see parallels between your journey and his?

Wyclef Jean: I would never have done some of the things I did without seeing a man like Ali do it first. When I was running, they were trying to give me a modern-day lynching. All I was trying to do was fight for a group of people that was voiceless. That’s what Ali did. And that’s what the Fugees stood for. We said we’re not going to just do music, we’re going to be a movement.

How do you keep going and not give up on people?

Wyclef Jean: No good deed goes unpunished. Nobody is telling you to do this. You make a commitment to the universe and to yourself. You keep going because you don’t expect anything in return. If you expect something in return, you’re not doing it for the right reasons.

Jay-Z, Kofi Black and the Quincy Jones rule

AllHipHop: Jay-Z is an executive producer on this, and you were just in London with him celebrating 30 years of “The Score.” How did it come together?

Wyclef Jean: We brought Jay-Z to London 30-something years ago, and one thing I love about Jay is you could do the littlest thing for him and he ain’t going to forget. When we were going off the stage, he looked at me and said, “Yo, keep going.” But my conversations on this were more with the director. You’re writing a theme that’s going to outlive you.

My biggest challenge was I did not want to sing it. I needed that David Ruffin voice, but young for today. I turned down a lot of people, some very famous. Then I remembered Kofi Black, a kid from the crew who’s half Ghanaian, half Jamaican. He does this crazy rendition of James Brown’s “It’s a Man’s Man’s Man’s World.” I woke him up out of his sleep and said, “Yo, I need you to sing this.”

AllHipHop: We don’t get theme songs like we used to. Think “Boomerang.” What’s happening?

Wyclef Jean: One of my greatest mentors is Quincy Jones. What I learned from Quincy is you have to write a theme song like a jam everybody is going to sing. So maybe with “Gladiator,” I’m bringing that swag back. You might be in the shower like, “I’m a gladiator.” I ran through “Sanford and Son,” “Good Times” and “Cheers” in my head. This is a family series, so I asked myself, if a 6-year-old is sitting there, what’s that melody?

The flag, family and staying curious

AllHipHop: What are two moments that make you proud?

Wyclef Jean: The first is 1996, when we won the Grammy and I put my Haitian flag over my shoulder. The world had never seen a Haitian flag like that on television. The next day, every Haitian kid who felt voiceless had a flag over their head.

In 2026, it’s having a daughter who’s 21, who walks into a room and shakes everyone’s hand. And a wife who’s still with me through thick and thin, and now we can smoke a cigar and laugh about it. Family and peace is the greatest thing for me.

AllHipHop: You’re still trending on social media in 2026. Did you ever think you’d still be talked about like this?

Wyclef Jean: I don’t think about it. If I did, maybe I wouldn’t be trending. I always tell the youth: Never lose your sense of curiosity. “The Score” was made in my uncle’s basement while people were going to the Hit Factory. Whether it’s Whitney Houston, Shakira or Beyoncé, I’m always the fan and the student in the room. That’s my secret sauce. I’m a forever curious student.

Seven albums, no boxes

AllHipHop: You promised seven albums this year. What’s next?

Wyclef Jean: Y’all thought I was capping. These are seven legacy pictures, my version of Quincy Jones’ “Back on the Block,” the seven genres I’ve touched. We’ve got “One Night in Kingston” coming next, the reggae album. My mama is still alive, and every time she sees me, she asks why I’m not singing gospel anymore. So No. 4 is Caribbean gospel, coming around Christmastime. And next year is the 30th anniversary of “The Carnival,” so look out for tours.

AllHipHop: What do you say to artists who feel boxed in, who only do R&B and feel like they can’t switch to country or gospel?

Wyclef Jean: The industry is playing a big game on everybody. They break music into categories, and when you break it into categories, you separate communities. When I played Kenny Rogers for people in the projects, they said, “This is hard.” I’m like, yeah, it’s country, but it’s really blues. Go back further, it’s Negro spirituals. There have always been Black people singing country music. The internet just showed everybody.

So don’t let nobody define you. No one can tell you who you are. If you like country but you’re scared because you’re doing trap right now, you’re not innovating. To be an innovator, you can’t keep the crowd comfortable.

AllHipHop: Do the Fugees have anything we can look forward to?

Wyclef Jean: Me and my sis are like two superheroes. We’re in a new era, and we’ve aligned spiritually and mentally. Whatever comes out is going to be enjoyable to y’all. But we’re not trying to do another “Score.” Many times people tried to put something together, and we never did that to y’all, because we know what “The Score” represents. It’s the new energy we’re on.

Thirty years after “The Score,” Jean is still doing what he says Ali taught him: following his gut, even when the crowd isn’t comfortable. Whether that’s a gospel album for his mother, a reggae record or a theme song built for a 6-year-old to sing, he’s not waiting for permission.

“Gladiator” by Wyclef Jean and Kofi Black is out now on Milan Records. “The Greatest” is streaming now on Prime Video.

item.title: All-White Quebec Rap Awards Slate Sparks Industry Backlash
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Quebec's ADISQ rap awards face backlash after all five album nominees were white, renewing questions about Black representation.
item.content:encoded:
Quebec’s biggest music-industry awards are facing a fresh argument over who gets recognized in rap after all five nominees in the 2026 album category were white.

The ADISQ slate named Aswell for Berger, Calamine for Rétrograde, FouKi for Still Kankan, Kinji00 for À la prochaine fois and Loud for Douze sur douze.

Loud won the category during the first gala on November 4. The result did not quiet the criticism.

Calamine had urged the eventual winner to recognize the Black artists who helped build Quebec’s rap scene. Loud followed that request when he accepted the award, turning the stage into an acknowledgment of the people missing from the ballot.

CBC’s video report on the dispute said Montreal artists viewed the all-white lineup as part of a longer problem with representation, not a one-night mistake.

The complaint goes beyond the identities of five performers. It raises questions about who enters the voting pool, which records reach decision-makers and how an awards system defines excellence in a genre created by Black artists.

The first gala was hosted by rapper Sarahmée, one of Quebec’s most visible Black artists.

That contrast sharpened the criticism: a Black woman could lead the ceremony while the rap-album ballot itself failed to include a single Black nominee.

ADISQ announced its broader 2026 nominations in September and handed out 46 trophies across its industry event and first gala.

Rap was only one piece of the program, but the makeup of that category quickly became one of the ceremony’s most pointed stories.

The tension is especially sharp because Quebec has a deep, multilingual rap community shaped by Black, immigrant and Francophone artists.

A category can include commercially established names and still leave listeners wondering whether the ballot reflects the full scene around it.

Canadian researchers have also examined anti-Black barriers in the country’s rap marketplace and awards culture. The ADISQ backlash gives that larger debate a current, concrete example: recognition can celebrate rap’s success while leaving its Black foundation outside the frame.

Neither Loud’s gesture nor the public criticism changes the official result.

Loud remains the 2026 winner, while the nominee list remains an all-white snapshot that artists and listeners are now asking ADISQ to explain.

item.title: Jeezy Taps Bill Bellamy For Sno Ball Gala To Fund Youth Programs
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jeezy announced his sixth Sno Ball Gala with host Bill Bellamy, raising money for youth business training and community programs.
item.content:encoded:
Jeezy is bringing his Sno Ball Gala back to Atlanta on November 10, with Bill Bellamy hosting a fundraiser for youth education, business training and community programs.

The sixth annual event will benefit the rapper’s Street Dreamz Foundation. Silent and live auctions will help raise money for its work in technology, entrepreneurship, health and financial literacy.

The foundation listed a 7 p.m. start at a private Atlanta location.

The announcement came as Jeezy’s team outlined where that support has been going.

According to the release sent to AllHipHop, the foundation joined Atlanta Life, SF and Goodr for a pop-up market that provided free groceries to 200 families.

It also worked with the Make-A-Wish Foundation to create experiences for children and their families.

Jeezy also served as the official program ambassador for Young CEO’s, an entrepreneurship initiative with the Urban League of Greater Atlanta.

The foundation described a 12-week program built around workshops, mentorship, business projects and networking. Participants work toward a pitch contest where they present their business ideas for support and recognition.

His involvement included taking part in an early pitch session and offering guidance to participants. The program’s stated goal is to help young people develop the skills to start businesses or move into leadership roles.

“I want to be more than just a mentor that they see every so often, but someone they can depend on daily,” Jeezy said in a statement on the foundation’s website.

Street Dreamz was founded in 2001. Its work has continued alongside the Atlanta rapper’s music career, with the gala giving supporters a way to fund programs beyond a single community event.

Last year, Jeezy announced a Community Day partnership with LISC in East Point, Georgia.

That event was planned around food distribution, school supplies, health screenings and resources for families, connecting the 20th anniversary of Let’s Get It: Thug Motivation 101 to his foundation’s work.

“It’s about making sure our neighborhoods have access to the same opportunities, the same capital, and the same future as anywhere else,” Jeezy said.

For this year’s Sno Ball, the foundation listed individual tickets at $1,000 and table sponsorships at $10,000.

Tickets and sponsorship information are available through the foundation’s Sno Ball event page.

Proceeds will support its youth programs, including financial education covering budgeting, saving, credit and investing.

item.title: Kid Cudi Calls Ye His Big Brother After Yeezy Runway Reunion
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kid Cudi praised Ye after the Yeezy Season 01 runway show, extending a reconciliation that returned them to the stage in September.
item.content:encoded:
Kid Cudi left Ye’s latest fashion show with no interest in reopening their old wounds.

The Cleveland rapper attended Yeezy Season 01 in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, joining a guest list that included Big Sean, 2 Chainz and designer Jerry Lorenzo.

When TMZ asked which part of the show stood out, Cudi answered, “Oh, everything.”

He also described Ye as his big brother and said he had been waiting to see Yeezy return to the runway.

The comments extend a reconciliation that became public in September. Cudi joined Ye at Soldier Field in Chicago, where the longtime collaborators performed together for the first time in years.

The reunion drew criticism because Ye had spent much of the previous year facing backlash over antisemitic statements and the song “Heil Hitler.”

Cudi did not retreat when radio host Peter Rosenberg challenged artists who were standing beside Ye.

“That man is my brother,” Cudi wrote at the time. “Damn near 2 decades of art and friendship.”

He added that Ye had apologized to him and said the apology felt sincere.

Their history stretches back to Cudi’s arrival at G.O.O.D. Music and includes the 2018 joint album Kids See Ghosts. It also includes several public breaks.

Their 2022 fallout centered on Cudi’s friendship with Pete Davidson while Davidson was dating Ye’s ex-wife Kim Kardashian.

Cudi later said in 2025 that he was finished with Ye after taking issue with comments about the late Virgil Abloh.

By this fall, the relationship had shifted again. The Chicago performance put them back onstage. Their appearance together at Wednesday’s show moved the reunion into Ye’s fashion world, where Cudi has also been a model and front-row presence over the years.

Yeezy Season 01 marked Ye’s first formal runway presentation since 2022.

All four of his children attended, along with Bianca Censori and several artists from his orbit. Models circled a large white structure at the new Yeezy flagship in Los Angeles as unreleased music played.

Cudi’s praise does not erase their past disputes, but it gives the reconciliation a clear public marker beyond the September concert.

He left the runway show talking about Ye as family, not a former collaborator.

item.title: Questlove Says He Sought Autism And ADHD Testing
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Questlove said he sought autism and ADHD testing while revisiting his childhood fascination with spinning records on IMO.
item.content:encoded:
Questlove said he sought testing for autism and ADHD about a year and a half ago, revisiting the childhood stories he once used to explain feeling different.

The Roots co-founder discussed the decision with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson on the November 4 episode of “IMO”.

“I decided to get tested for autism, ADHD, like a year and a half ago,” Questlove said.

He said he had long described himself as “the outcast or the black sheep.”

He framed the account as a “quasi disclosure.”

The discussion turned to his childhood fascination with spinning objects, including records on a turntable.

Recounting a story from his mother, he said an aunt watched him stare at a rotating record for roughly 20 minutes before any music played.

He also recalled a spinning light above his bed that calmed him. He joked that the way a label looked as it spun shaped some of the music he gravitated toward, even before the songs themselves.

Those memories had come up publicly years before.

During a 2013 Fresh Air conversation about his memoir Mo’ Meta Blues, Questlove described relatives wondering why he could spend hours watching records turn.

He said he also spun his father’s records on his index finger.

“I liked the way the logo looked in rotation. They just thought that was kind of strange,” he told Terry Gross.

In that earlier discussion, Gross asked about autism after referring to a passage in his memoir.

Questlove described his family’s concerns and said some of the discussion had involved joking. The exchange did not establish a diagnosis.

His childhood also put him inside the music business early.

His father, the legendary singer Lee Andrews of Lee Andrews & The Hearts, took him on the road.

Questlove told Gross he learned to handle wardrobe and stage lights before filling in on drums at Radio City Music Hall at 12.

That lifelong interest in music history continued with his 2026 documentary “Earth, Wind & Fire (To Be Celestial vs. That’s the Weight of the World)”.

Produced and directed by Questlove, the HBO film debuted June 7. It traced the band through late founder Maurice White and explored the spiritual ideas behind its music.
